title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Trauma — September 2026

studies.title: Common mental disorders are lasting longer than they did a decade ago
studies.ns_score_reason: a big, well-designed national cohort with a genuinely unexpected explanation for rising mental illness rates; limited by diagnostic-interview reliance.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers used the third Netherlands Mental Health Survey and Incidence Study (NEMESIS-3; N=6,194, aged 18–75, interviewed 2019–2022 and again 2023–2024) to measure how often anxiety, mood, and substance use disorders were still present three years later, then compared those rates with the same measurements taken 12 years earlier in NEMESIS-2 (N=6,646). Persistence of any common mental disorder rose from 42.7% to 57.9% across the two cohorts. Younger age, city living, childhood trauma, and near-daily drug use all predicted greater persistence — and those predictors were stable over the 12 years.
studies.why_it_matters: The widely reported rise in mental ill health may be less about more people falling ill and more about fewer people getting better — a different problem, with different implications for how treatment and long-term care are organized.
studies.pitch_angle: Everyone assumes the mental health crisis is about incidence. This Dutch cohort suggests the disorders themselves have become stickier — more than half of people with an anxiety, mood, or substance disorder still met criteria three years on, up sharply from the same survey a decade earlier. Open on the paradox of expanding treatment access alongside falling recovery rates, and call Brenda Penninx or Margreet ten Have at the Trimbos Institute. Note that childhood trauma was among the strongest predictors of a disorder that refuses to lift.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health-policy or general-interest outlet on "recovery rates as the missing metric" — mental health systems count how many people are treated, almost never how many stay well, and the Dutch data show what happens when you actually look.
studies.caveats: Observational design (cannot establish causation); diagnoses via structured interview (CIDI 3.0) rather than clinical assessment; comparison across two cohorts uses partly different DSM criteria; Netherlands-specific and may not generalize.

studies.title: Mass shooting survivors describe time slowing down as they ran
studies.ns_score_reason: rare, ethically difficult data on how memory works during extreme threat; small N and qualitative design cap it.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed written narratives from 42 survivors (74% women; mean age 42.1) of the Route 91 Harvest Festival shooting in Las Vegas, collected within one month of the event. A codebook thematic analysis identified four recurring structures: richly detailed contextual memory (sensory-perceptual features, space, time), physical injury, heroism, and contemplating mortality. Survivors reported vivid sensory impressions and spatial awareness organized around escape routes, alongside temporal distortions including subjective slowing and gaps in the sequence of events.
studies.why_it_matters: Almost all laboratory work on memory under threat uses proxies; this is one of the very few structured looks at what people actually encode during a real mass-casualty event, and it suggests memory reorganizes around survival action rather than around the timeline.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the time distortion — survivors consistently described the shooting unfolding in slow motion while whole chunks of sequence vanished, a combination that maps onto how spatial escape planning appears to dominate encoding. Open on a survivor tracing their route out of the festival grounds. Worth calling Colleen Parks at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and Charles Morgan III at Yale, who has studied memory under extreme military stress. Keep well clear of implying anything about the reliability of eyewitness testimony from these data alone.
studies.wider_angle: For a long-form or criminal-justice outlet: what mass shooting survivors remember versus what investigators need them to remember, and the gap that creates in the days after an attack.
studies.caveats: Small N (42); prompted rather than free recall; written self-report allowing revision; predominantly female sample; no comparison group; single event.

studies.title: Judges deciding sexual abuse cases still rely on cues that science has discredited
studies.ns_score_reason: combines a professional survey with a large document analysis of real rulings, and the finding has direct real-world stakes.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In Study 1, 79 Dutch legal professionals were surveyed about which criteria they use to judge a witness statement's credibility: consistency (66%), accuracy (66%), and detailedness (53%) dominated, but nonverbal behavior (14%), displayed emotion (13%), and "authentic impression" (11%) also featured. In Study 2, the team analyzed 518 Dutch court rulings on sexual assault, finding the same content criteria in the lead — consistency 80.1%, detailedness 65%, accuracy 31% — alongside authentic impression (23%), emotionality during the statement (13%), and "signs of trauma" (9.5%). Only 13% of rulings drew on all three content criteria, indicating unsystematic application.
studies.why_it_matters: Decades of memory research show that demeanor, displayed emotion, and apparent trauma are poor guides to whether an account is truthful, yet they are turning up in real verdicts in a country with a well-regarded judiciary.
studies.pitch_angle: Sell the number: nearly a quarter of 518 sexual assault rulings invoked how "authentic" the witness seemed. Open in a courtroom where a survivor's flat affect is read as coolness rather than as a known trauma response, then bring in what the memory literature actually says about consistency and detail as credibility markers. Bruno Verschuere at the University of Amsterdam is the call. Frame it as a question about judicial training, not as a claim that specific verdicts were wrong.
studies.wider_angle: For a law or investigative outlet: the credibility gap in sexual offense trials across Europe, and whether structured, validated statement-assessment tools should be mandated in judicial training — with the Dutch rulings as the evidence base.
studies.caveats: Netherlands-specific legal system; ruling text may not fully capture judges' reasoning; survey sample modest (N=79) and self-selected; no outcome data on whether reliance on weak criteria produced wrong verdicts.

studies.title: Psychiatric diagnoses barely predict how patients actually fare
studies.ns_score_reason: striking numbers from a decent clinical sample, but the outcome measures are largely self-report and one author has a royalty interest in a measure used.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using assessment data from 685 outpatients at an academic medical center, researchers tested whether categorical psychiatric diagnoses or transdiagnostic dimensions (fear/distress, narcissistic antagonism, attachment, flexible thinking, somatization, external coping, anger/aggression) better predicted five outcomes. Diagnoses alone predicted only pain (R²=0.08) and failed to predict suicidal ideation, cognitive concerns, psychosocial functioning, or quality of life. Adding dimensions transformed every model — psychosocial functioning ΔR²=0.55, suicidal ideation ΔR²=0.41, quality of life ΔR²=0.38 — with somatization the single most robust predictor. Notably, when the order was reversed, a trauma diagnosis was the one category that added meaningfully to the dimensions in predicting suicidal ideation.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers hard numbers to the argument that diagnostic labels tell you surprisingly little about a person's life, while dimensional traits tell you a great deal — with trauma standing out as the exception that still carries independent weight.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the near-zero: your diagnosis explained essentially none of the variance in whether you were suicidal, functioning, or satisfied with life — but seven trait dimensions explained up to 55%. Open on a patient collecting labels over a decade of care while nothing about their day-to-day changes. Call Emily Dowgwillo at the University of Detroit Mercy. Flag the trauma exception: it was the one diagnostic category that added predictive value on its own.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist psychiatry or science-policy outlet: the slow-motion replacement of DSM categories by dimensional frameworks (HiTOP, RDoC), and what happens to insurance, research funding, and drug trials if the categories go.
studies.caveats: Single-center; cross-sectional; outcomes largely self-reported; industry-adjacent conflict — co-author Mark Blais receives royalties on the SPECTRA measure used to derive dimensions; treatment-seeking outpatients may not generalize.

studies.title: Depression may come first and drive complex PTSD, not the other way around
studies.ns_score_reason: four waves over two years with a within-person model is strong design; the population is highly specific.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 250 "de facto unattended children" in China — children whose parents are dead, missing, imprisoned, or too ill or disabled to provide care — across four waves over two years, applying a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model to separate within-person change from stable between-person differences. Depressive symptoms were longitudinally associated with later PTSD and, more strongly, with disturbances in self-organization (DSO), the emotional-regulation and self-concept cluster that distinguishes complex PTSD. DSO in turn predicted depressive symptoms from wave 2 onward, suggesting a self-sustaining loop rather than a one-way street.
studies.why_it_matters: The clinical default is that trauma symptoms drive secondary depression; this suggests depression may help generate complex PTSD in chronically traumatized children, which would change what you treat first.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the reversal — in children living without effective guardianship, low mood appeared to feed the emergence of complex PTSD rather than trailing behind it, with emotional dysregulation as the hinge. Open on the scale of the unattended-children population in China, a group barely visible in the trauma literature. Juzhe Xi at East China Normal University is the contact. Be explicit that this is within-person association over time, not proof of causation.
studies.wider_angle: For a global health or development outlet: children raised in the gaps of the family system — parental imprisonment, chronic illness, migration — and why the mental health data on them is so thin worldwide.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation); self-report symptom measures; highly specific population unlikely to generalize; attrition across four waves not detailed in the abstract.

studies.title: Veterans who broke their own moral code report more feelings of unreality
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean, specific finding on a much-discussed but under-measured concept; cross-sectional and self-report.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A volunteer sample of 189 Israeli male combat veterans completed validated measures of PTSD symptoms, exposure to potentially morally injurious events (PMIEs), and dissociative symptoms. PTSD symptoms clustered with depersonalization and derealization, supporting a dissociative subtype, and mediated the link between moral injury exposure and dissociation. Crucially, one specific facet — having committed moral transgressions oneself, as opposed to witnessing or being betrayed — was independently associated with depersonalization and derealization.
studies.why_it_matters: Moral injury has been discussed largely as guilt and shame; this points to a distinct route in which acts one committed are associated with feeling detached from one's own body and surroundings, which would call for different treatment than fear-based PTSD.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is the asymmetry: what a soldier did, not what was done to them, tracked with feeling unreal. Open on the clinical picture of a veteran who describes watching himself from outside during and long after deployment. Call Doron Potik at Ashkelon Academic College. Note that this is an association in a self-selected sample, not evidence that treating dissociation will resolve moral injury.
studies.wider_angle: For a defense or long-form outlet: moral injury is becoming a formal target of military mental health services in several countries, and the question of whether perpetration-based injury needs its own treatment pathway — including for drone operators and remote combatants.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); all self-report; volunteer sample of male combat veterans in one country; mediation inferred from cross-sectional data.

studies.title: Whether you "have PTSD" can depend on which scoring rule your clinician uses
studies.ns_score_reason: a diagnostic-instrument paper, but the headline number (18% to 38%) is genuinely arresting and validated against clinician interviews.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers assessed 248 trauma-exposed Swedish adults (mean age 36.5, 79% female) with both the clinician-administered CAPS-5 and the self-report PCL-5. The questionnaire showed good internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and convergent validity — but limited specificity against other internalizing problems. Most striking: applying different symptom-cluster models to the same responses produced probable PTSD rates ranging from 18% to 38%, and threshold scores of 31–33 gave the best sensitivity–specificity balance, well away from a single universal cut-off.
studies.why_it_matters: The most widely used PTSD self-report instrument in the world can roughly double the number of people it flags depending on defensible choices about how symptoms are grouped — a quiet source of variation in prevalence estimates and in who gets referred.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the doubling. Same 248 people, same answers, and a diagnosis rate that swings from 18% to 38% based on the scoring model. Frame it against New Scientist's existing thread about how we decide what counts as trauma, and open on the moment a screening score decides whether someone enters a treatment pathway. Karin Bondjers and Filip Arnberg at Uppsala University's National Centre for Disaster Psychiatry are the calls.
studies.wider_angle: For a metascience or health-statistics outlet: how much of the reported global variation in PTSD prevalence is real and how much is instrument bookkeeping — a piece that could also take in depression and anxiety screening cut-offs.
studies.caveats: Single-country sample; predominantly female; authors describe threshold estimates as preliminary and requiring replication in larger samples; no external validation cohort.

studies.title: Avoidance may be the weakest sign of PTSD in refugees
studies.ns_score_reason: challenges a core diagnostic assumption in a decent-sized sample, but the design is cross-sectional questionnaire modeling.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 267 trauma-exposed young adults with a refugee background living in Sweden (61% male, mean age 25.2), using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling to test how each PTSD symptom cluster contributes to the overall construct and how each relates to psychological resilience. Hyperarousal, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and re-experiencing were all stronger indicators of PTSD than avoidance. Resilience was strongly and negatively associated with hyperarousal and negative alterations in mood, but showed no significant association with avoidance.
studies.why_it_matters: Avoidance is a required criterion for a DSM-5 PTSD diagnosis; if it carries little weight in a refugee population where threat is ongoing rather than past, some people may be assessed against a template built for a different situation.
studies.pitch_angle: Sell the diagnostic mismatch: the symptom cluster you must have to be diagnosed with PTSD was the least informative one in this refugee sample, while hyperarousal — plausibly a rational response to continuing insecurity about status, housing, and family — dominated. Open on the difference between remembering danger and still living in it. Gerhard Andersson at Linköping University is the call.
studies.wider_angle: For a global health or anthropology-leaning outlet: the long-running argument over whether Western PTSD criteria travel, revisited with data rather than assertion, and what culturally grounded assessment would actually look like.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); all self-report; single host country; heterogeneous countries of origin collapsed into one group; young adults only.

studies.title: Childhood maltreatment predicts depression severity — inflammation does not
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean null against a fashionable hypothesis in an unusually pure sample, but N is modest and the sample's narrow BMI range may explain the null.
studies.the_study: Researchers assessed 133 first-episode, drug-naïve patients with major depression in Turkey — a rare sample, uncontaminated by prior medication — measuring childhood maltreatment, circadian preference, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein against both self-rated and clinician-rated depression severity. Childhood maltreatment was consistently associated with severity on both scales (β=0.362 and 0.288). Evening chronotype was associated with self-rated severity only. hs-CRP showed no independent association with depression severity on either measure; body mass index was the strongest correlate of CRP.
studies.why_it_matters: The inflammation-causes-depression story has become popular well beyond psychiatry; in patients at the very start of illness and never exposed to antidepressants, the association did not hold, while early adversity did.
studies.pitch_angle: The lead is the null. In a sample designed to be as clean as psychiatric research gets — first episode, never medicated — the inflammatory marker everyone talks about tracked body weight, not depression, whereas childhood maltreatment tracked severity on every measure. Open on the popular framing of "inflamed brains" and then this result. Call the Eskişehir City Hospital psychiatry group. Note that a narrow BMI distribution in this sample limits what a null can prove.
studies.wider_angle: For a general-interest health outlet: what happens to a biomarker hypothesis when you strip out confounds — a piece on how obesity, medication, and chronic illness may have inflated the apparent depression–inflammation link across the literature.
studies.caveats: Small-to-modest N (133); cross-sectional; single-center; participants with hs-CRP ≥10 mg/L excluded; narrow BMI distribution may have masked a real association; childhood maltreatment measured retrospectively by questionnaire.

studies.title: A history of childhood adversity doesn't stop chronic pain treatment working
studies.ns_score_reason: a reasonably sized longitudinal cohort with a hopeful, nuanced result; no control group and a specialist inpatient setting.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 324 inpatients through a five-week interdisciplinary pain rehabilitation program in Germany, grouping them by adverse childhood experiences (none, 1–3, four or more). A striking 83.3% reported at least one ACE and 18.5% reported four or more. Those with more ACEs started with higher depression, anxiety, stress, and pain-related incapability — emotional abuse was a particularly strong predictor — but all groups improved significantly over the program, with the high-ACE group still ending at higher absolute distress.
studies.why_it_matters: It complicates the fatalistic reading of the ACE literature: early adversity set the starting point, not the slope of recovery, in this pain rehabilitation setting.
studies.pitch_angle: The reader-facing surprise is that people carrying four or more childhood adversities improved as much as everyone else — they simply began further back. Open on the 83% figure in a pain clinic, which is itself worth a paragraph. Call Franziska Kessemeier at Witten/Herdecke University. Resist framing this as "trauma causes chronic pain"; the design cannot show that.
studies.wider_angle: For a medical or health-services outlet: the case for routinely asking about childhood adversity in pain clinics, and the ethical and practical questions that follow — who asks, what happens to the answer, and whether trauma-informed pain care changes anything measurable.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort with no control group; single rehabilitation center; ACEs assessed retrospectively by questionnaire; self-reported outcomes; short follow-up (end of a five-week program).

studies.title: A 17-minute video handed out during a forensic exam may help after sexual assault
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely novel intervention point and a randomized SMART design, but this is a feasibility study with no efficacy claim.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Fifty women aged 18 and over who presented for a Sexual Assault Medical Forensic Exam within seven days of an assault were randomized in a Sequential Multiple Assignment Randomized Trial to receive a 17-minute video, Skills Training in Affective Recovery (STAR), or no video. At one week, those above threshold on acute stress or opioid use (n=36) were randomized again to a 21-day text message program (TextSTAR) or none. Acceptability was high — 80% who saw STAR rated it extremely acceptable — and retention was 94% at one week and 90% at four weeks.
studies.why_it_matters: The hours immediately after an assault are one of the few moments almost every survivor is in contact with a health system, and almost nothing is currently delivered then; this shows an intervention at that point is at least deliverable and welcome.
studies.pitch_angle: New Scientist has covered the idea that what you do in the first hours after trauma may shape what comes later — the Tetris work being the obvious precedent. Here the window is a forensic exam room, the intervention is a short video plus three weeks of texts, and survivors overwhelmingly accepted it. Open in the exam room. Call Kate Walsh at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Be clear that this trial tested feasibility, not whether symptoms improved.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-services or women's health outlet: the sexual assault forensic exam as a missed public health touchpoint, and what else — opioid risk counseling, follow-up scheduling — could be built into it.
studies.caveats: Small N (50, then 36); feasibility and acceptability outcomes only, no efficacy conclusions; self-reported symptom measures; women only; short follow-up (four weeks); multi-site but US-specific service context.

studies.title: A new screening tool aims to catch PTSD that starts in pregnancy, not just at birth
studies.journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: fills a real gap in universal perinatal screening, but development-stage psychometrics on a small sample.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (1 hits)
studies.the_study: Australian researchers developed a screening instrument for post-traumatic stress arising anywhere across the perinatal period — conception, pregnancy, or postpartum — rather than only after childbirth. Twenty-five candidate items were tested by exploratory factor analysis (n=114), yielding a 17-item, two-factor tool explaining 68.36% of variance with excellent internal consistency (α=.954 and .897). Against semi-structured clinical interviews (n=52), a cutoff of ≥11 gave 90.9% sensitivity and 61% specificity.
studies.why_it_matters: Universal perinatal mental health screening in Australia asks about depression and anxiety but not trauma, so PTSD following miscarriage, fertility treatment, or a frightening pregnancy is routinely missed.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is what current screening doesn't ask. Open on a woman screened repeatedly through pregnancy for low mood while intrusive memories of an earlier loss go unrecorded. Call Sarah Medland at QIMR Berghofer or Tanya Mackle at Metro North Mental Health. The specificity of 61% is worth being honest about — this is a net designed to over-catch, and the authors say validation is pending.
studies.wider_angle: For a parenting or women's health outlet: the widening definition of birth trauma, including partners and fathers, and how services in the UK, Australia, and the US are and aren't adapting.
studies.caveats: Small N (114 for factor analysis, 52 for ROC); single-country; development-stage tool awaiting independent validation; modest specificity; self-selected participants who endorsed perinatal trauma.

studies.title: Neglect, not the drinking itself, links parental substance abuse to child exploitation
studies.ns_score_reason: a large sample from a population almost absent from the literature; cross-sectional self-report and a difficult data-collection context.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Working in urban slums of Lahore, Pakistan, the researcher collected data from 738 children aged 10–18 directly exposed to paternal substance abuse, and used structural equation modeling to test how that exposure relates to sexual exploitation and emotional dysregulation. Paternal substance abuse was strongly associated with caregiver neglect, and neglect statistically mediated the relationship between paternal substance abuse and both child sexual exploitation and emotional dysregulation. Controlling for child gender barely altered the model.
studies.why_it_matters: It identifies a specific, addressable link in the chain — supervision and caregiving capacity — rather than treating parental addiction as an undifferentiated risk factor, in a population where child protection research is scarce.
studies.pitch_angle: The finding worth leading on is the mediator: it wasn't the father's substance use that tracked with exploitation so much as the collapse of supervision that followed it, meaning a father's addiction and a child's risk are separated by an intervenable step. Open in a Lahore slum neighborhood. Call Tanveer Abdullah at the University of Peshawar. Handle sensitively — these are children reporting on exploitation.
studies.wider_angle: For a global development or international news outlet: how child protection systems are designed almost entirely around parental intent, when the mechanism that harms children most often is absence of supervision — with implications from Lahore to Glasgow.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); self-reported by children; single-city convenience sample; sensitive outcomes likely under-reported; mediation inferred from cross-sectional data.

studies.title: Rejection and violence, not everyday discrimination, drive trauma symptoms in trans people
studies.ns_score_reason: first meta-analysis of its kind and highly timely, but built on only 10 unique samples.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted a PRISMA-guided meta-analysis of studies using the Gender Minority Stress and Resilience measure alongside post-traumatic stress symptoms, identifying 13 sources representing 10 unique samples. Rejection (r=.39) and violence (r=.36) showed moderate mean associations with post-traumatic stress symptoms, while discrimination showed a smaller association (r=.25). The authors argue these stressors sit outside the conventional Criterion A definition of a traumatic event yet track with trauma symptoms at meaningful magnitudes.
studies.why_it_matters: It bears directly on the live question of what should count as trauma: experiences that don't meet the diagnostic threshold for a traumatic event nonetheless show associations with post-traumatic stress symptoms comparable in size to many recognized stressors.
studies.pitch_angle: Pitch this straight into the "how do we decide what counts as trauma" debate. The measurable ordering — rejection and violence well ahead of discrimination — is the specific, reportable finding, and it suggests interpersonal severing matters more than institutional slights. Open on the diagnostic manual's Criterion A and what it excludes. Call Francesca Kassing at Alliant International University. Stick to association; none of these are longitudinal.
studies.wider_angle: For a social-science or policy outlet: minority stress as a public health exposure, and whether the health effects of legislation aimed at a group can be tracked epidemiologically the way air pollution is.
studies.caveats: Only 10 unique samples; all constituent studies cross-sectional and self-report; heterogeneous samples, mostly US-based; small evidence base means effect estimates are unstable; no causal inference possible.

studies.title: Earthquake survivors who build a "trauma identity" fare worse
studies.journal: Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice
studies.ns_score_reason: a relatable psychological mechanism tested in a real disaster population; cross-sectional SEM limits causal reading.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 285 adults (65.3% female) who lived through the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes in Türkiye, testing structural models of PTSD and complex PTSD. Trauma memories predicted post-traumatic cognitions, which in turn predicted both a "trauma identity" — the sense that the event has become who you are — and safety-seeking behaviors; both then linked to symptoms and worse mental health. Trauma identity carried more weight in the PTSD model, while safety-seeking behaviors dominated in the complex PTSD model.
studies.why_it_matters: It separates two familiar responses to disaster — reorganizing your sense of self around the event, versus reorganizing your daily behavior around avoiding danger — and suggests they feed different symptom profiles.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the distinction readers will recognize in themselves: some people become the thing that happened to them, others just keep checking the exits. Open on a survivor who still sleeps fully dressed. Call İsmail Seçer at Atatürk University. Note carefully that this is cross-sectional modeling — the arrows in the diagram are hypotheses, not demonstrated causation.
studies.wider_angle: For a psychology-focused or long-form outlet: the rise of "trauma identity" in popular culture and online communities, and what the clinical evidence actually says about identifying with what happened to you.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); all self-report; single disaster and country; female-skewed sample; SEM path direction assumed rather than tested.

studies.title: Trouble naming your feelings may link childhood trauma to a stiffer heartbeat
studies.ns_score_reason: an appealing mind-body chain with an objective physiological outcome, but small, cross-sectional, and in students.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In 152 Chinese university students (mean age 22.2), researchers measured childhood adversity, alexithymia (difficulty identifying and describing emotions), anxiety symptoms, and heart rate variability derived from electrocardiogram recordings. Higher childhood trauma scores were associated with lower HRV, an index of autonomic flexibility. Serial mediation analysis indicated that alexithymia and anxiety accounted for the association both independently and in sequence.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers a candidate psychological route — impaired emotional awareness — for the well-documented but poorly explained link between early adversity and altered autonomic function, though the design cannot test whether the sequence runs that way.
studies.pitch_angle: The interesting claim is that the body's stress-regulation signature may run partly through whether you can name what you are feeling — not just through the adversity itself. Open on alexithymia as a trait most people have never heard of but will recognize. Call Zhi-Jun Xiao at Southern Medical University. Do not let this become "childhood trauma damages your heart"; it is an association in 152 students.
studies.wider_angle: For a health or wellness-skeptical outlet: heart rate variability has become a consumer metric on every fitness tracker — a piece on what HRV actually indexes, what it doesn't, and why the psychology behind it is messier than the app suggests.
studies.caveats: Small N (152); cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); university students only, unlikely to generalize; retrospective self-report of childhood adversity; serial mediation inferred from a single time point.

studies.title: How a therapist asks questions changes the trauma story a client tells
studies.ns_score_reason: a sensitive, well-motivated question about therapeutic influence on narrative, but purely qualitative with no measure of accuracy.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 62 therapy sessions and 24 client interviews with refugees and immigrants from Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, and Lebanon receiving trauma therapy in Isfahan, Iran, combining micro-level discourse analysis of therapist prompts with macro-level analysis of how narratives changed across sessions. Interpretive questions and reformulations by therapists were associated with shifts in the temporal sequencing, evaluative framing, and coherence of clients' trauma narratives; open-ended prompts and reflective listening were associated with clients elaborating more autonomously. Multilingual switching and culturally patterned storytelling also shaped how narratives stabilized.
studies.why_it_matters: It documents, at the level of individual conversational turns, how the shape of a trauma account can shift in response to how it is elicited — a process rarely observed directly, and one with obvious ethical weight in asylum and legal contexts.
studies.pitch_angle: The uncomfortable observation here is that a therapist reformulating a client's sentence can be followed by a change in how the client sequences and evaluates the event. Open on a session where a question rearranges a timeline. Note explicitly that the researchers studied coherence and stabilization, not accuracy, and were careful to say so. Contact Masoud Mahmoudi-Dehaki at Islamic Azad University.
studies.wider_angle: For a legal or immigration-focused outlet: asylum decisions often hinge on whether an applicant tells a consistent story across retellings, while this work suggests retelling in supportive settings reliably reshapes narratives — a direct tension worth reporting out with immigration lawyers.
studies.caveats: Qualitative, no control condition or quantitative outcome; single clinical site in Iran; no measure of memory accuracy; therapist and client selection unspecified; findings may not generalize to other therapeutic modalities or languages.

studies.title: Who drops out of trauma treatment isn't predicted by how ill they are
studies.journal: International Journal of Psychiatry in Clinical Practice
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful negative result about symptom severity, but small, single-facility, and retrospective.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers examined 76 women hospitalized between 2019 and 2023 at an Israeli inpatient facility treating PTSD and eating disorders (96% had PTSD, 74% an eating disorder, 70% both). Fully 43.4% left treatment prematurely. Dropout was associated with sexual risk-taking behaviors, impulsive departures during the admission, and — counterintuitively — fewer prior hospitalizations, while no sociodemographic variable or symptom severity score distinguished those who left. Those who left and later returned had outcomes comparable to those who stayed throughout.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests dropout from intensive trauma treatment is a behavioral and relational event rather than a marker of being too unwell, and that services which allow people back after a rupture may not lose much.
studies.pitch_angle: Nearly half walked out, and nothing on the admission paperwork predicted who. What did predict it was impulsive behavior during the stay — and, encouragingly, those who returned did as well as those who never left. Open on the moment a patient walks out of an inpatient unit. Call Jonathan Handelzalts at the Academic College of Tel-Aviv-Yaffo. Frame carefully: this is a small retrospective sample, not a template for service design.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-services outlet: the "one strike" discharge policy common in intensive mental health and addiction treatment, and the emerging evidence that treating disengagement as a rupture to be repaired rather than a failure to be punished may retain more people.
studies.caveats: Small N (76); single-center; women only; retrospective chart-based design; observational (cannot establish causation); no long-term follow-up after discharge.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Six studies in this batch, from very different angles, all show that the boundary of "PTSD" is set by measurement choices rather than by anything stable in patients. Applying different symptom-cluster models to the same 248 Swedish respondents moved probable PTSD from 18% to 38% ("Whether you 'have PTSD' can depend on which scoring rule your clinician uses", PMID 42635035); avoidance — a required DSM-5 criterion — was the weakest indicator of the construct in refugees still living with ongoing threat (PMID 42635367); rejection and violence against trans people, which fall outside Criterion A altogether, tracked post-traumatic stress at r=.39 and .36 (PMID 42658623); categorical diagnoses explained almost none of the variance in patients' functioning or suicidal ideation, with trauma the one label that still carried independent weight (PMID 42644771); a new Australian instrument exists precisely because perinatal screening never asks about trauma (PMID 41936021); and Dutch judges are reading "signs of trauma" and "authentic impression" into sexual assault verdicts in 518 rulings (PMID 41308177). Two further papers show the account itself is malleable: therapist prompts reshaped how refugee clients sequenced and framed events (PMID 42684797), and "trauma identity" behaved as a distinct mechanism in earthquake survivors (PMID 42036873).

**Why pitch this now:** Prevalence figures, service thresholds, asylum decisions and criminal verdicts are all being made on the basis of a category that, on this month's evidence, can nearly double or halve depending on defensible technical choices — and the popular expansion of "trauma" is running ahead of any settled definition.

**Angle:** Follow one construct through the machinery that uses it — screening questionnaire, clinic threshold, courtroom, asylum interview — showing at each stop how much slack there is in deciding who counts as traumatized, and who gains or loses by where the line falls. Aimed at general science readers who have absorbed trauma language from culture but never seen how the diagnosis is actually manufactured.

**Potential headlines:**
- The scoring rule that doubles how many people have PTSD
- Trauma's problem isn't that it is over-diagnosed — it is that nobody agrees where it starts
- Whether your trauma counts depends on who is holding the questionnaire

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Mind** — sits directly in its running thread on how we decide what counts as trauma, and the 18%-to-38% figure gives it a hard news spine.
- **Undark** — well suited to a reported piece on measurement instruments quietly shaping who gets care, including the courtroom and asylum strands.
- **STAT** — the diagnostic-categories-versus-dimensions material (PMID 42644771) and screening thresholds have direct consequences for reimbursement, referral and trials.
- **The Guardian science desk** — would take the justice angle, with Dutch rulings invoking "signs of trauma" and the asylum-consistency tension as the news peg.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Trauma — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-04 | **Studies reviewed:** 18
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-09-04

### Study 1: Common mental disorders are lasting longer than they did a decade ago
**PMID:** 42687372 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Core numbers check out: N = 6,194 (18–75, interviewed 2019–2022 and 2023–2024), NEMESIS-2 N = 6,646, broad persistence 42.7% → 57.9%, and the four significant determinants.

**Issue A. Predictors presented as ranked** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Note that childhood trauma was among the strongest predictors of a disorder that refuses to lift."
- **Abstract says:** "Higher broad persistence was significantly associated with younger age, living in a city, childhood trauma, and near-daily drug use in multivariable analyses."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports four significant associations without ranking their magnitude. "Among the strongest" is not supported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that childhood trauma was one of four factors significantly associated with greater persistence."

**Issue B. Cohort-comparison description** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "comparison across two cohorts uses partly different DSM criteria"
- **Abstract says:** "Twelve-year trends were examined by comparing DSM-IV persistence in NEMESIS-3 with NEMESIS-2 (N = 6,646; interviewed 2007-2009 and 2010-2012) among adults aged 18-64 years."
- **Problem:** The 12-year comparison was deliberately restricted to DSM-IV diagnoses in both cohorts, so the caveat misdescribes the design. The real restriction the digest omits is that the trend comparison covers ages 18–64 only, not the full 18–75 sample.
- **Suggested fix:** "the 12-year trend comparison uses DSM-IV criteria in both cohorts and is restricted to adults aged 18–64"

**Issue C. Incidence-versus-persistence framing** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The widely reported rise in mental ill health may be less about more people falling ill and more about fewer people getting better"
- **Abstract says:** "Recent increases in common mental disorder prevalence could partly reflect greater persistence of existing disorders."
- **Problem:** The study measured persistence only; it did not compare incidence trends, so it cannot apportion the rise between the two. The abstract's "could partly reflect" is weaker than the digest's either/or tilt.
- **Suggested fix:** "The widely reported rise in mental ill health may partly reflect existing disorders lasting longer, not just more people falling ill"

---

### Study 2: Mass shooting survivors describe time slowing down as they ran
**PMID:** 42647049 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 42, 74% women, mean age 42.1, within one month, four themes, subjective slowing and sequence gaps — all accurate.

**Issue A. Claims about what dominates encoding** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "it suggests memory reorganizes around survival action rather than around the timeline" and "a combination that maps onto how spatial escape planning appears to dominate encoding"
- **Abstract says:** "Survivors recalled vivid sensory impressions, detailed spatial awareness organized around escape, and temporal distortions, including both subjective slowing and sequence gaps."
- **Problem:** A codebook thematic analysis of 42 narratives with no comparison group cannot establish that one form of content dominates another, or that memory is "reorganized" relative to some baseline. These are themes identified in prompted written accounts, not measured relative weights.
- **Suggested fix:** "it is one of the very few structured looks at what people describe encoding during a real mass-casualty event, and escape-related spatial detail sat alongside distorted time in survivors' accounts"

**Issue B. "Consistently"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "survivors consistently described the shooting unfolding in slow motion while whole chunks of sequence vanished"
- **Abstract says:** "temporal distortions, including both subjective slowing and sequence gaps" were part of the contextual-memory theme.
- **Problem:** Thematic prevalence isn't quantified in the abstract; "consistently" implies near-universal endorsement.
- **Suggested fix:** "survivors described the shooting unfolding in slow motion alongside gaps in the sequence of events"

**Issue C. NS fit score** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "NS fit:** 7/10"
- **Problem:** The evidence base is 42 prompted, written self-reports, predominantly female, single event, no comparison group, and purely qualitative. The rarity of the sample is genuine, but a 7 overstates the evidential weight for a Mind feature built on interpretive claims about encoding.
- **Suggested fix:** "NS fit:** 6/10 — rare, ethically difficult data on what survivors report from an extreme event; qualitative, prompted self-report with no comparison group."

---

### Study 3: Judges deciding sexual abuse cases still rely on cues that science has discredited
**PMID:** 41308177 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

All percentages from both studies match the abstract exactly, including the 13% relying on all three content criteria.

**Issue A. "Discredited" overstates the abstract's language** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "cues that science has discredited" / "Decades of memory research show that demeanor, displayed emotion, and apparent trauma are poor guides to whether an account is truthful"
- **Abstract says:** "Highly contested criteria (i.e., emotion, trauma, nonverbal behaviour, authentic impression) are also regularly used."
- **Problem:** The authors describe these criteria as "highly contested," not discredited, and the abstract does not characterize the state of the evidence base. The digest asserts settled consensus.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Judges deciding sexual abuse cases still rely on contested credibility cues"; body: "The criteria the authors call highly contested — demeanour, displayed emotion, apparent trauma — are turning up in real verdicts."

**Issue B. Published erratum not noted** — Severity: Minor

- **Abstract says:** "Erratum in Memory. 2026 May;34(5):608. doi: 10.1080/09658211.2026.2643966."
- **Problem:** The digest cites percentages from an article that carries a subsequent erratum; the digest does not flag this. Whether the erratum touches any reported figure is unverifiable from the abstract alone.
- **Suggested fix:** Add to Caveats: "A published erratum (Memory 2026;34(5):608) exists — check the correction before quoting figures."

---

### Study 4: Psychiatric diagnoses barely predict how patients actually fare
**PMID:** 42644771 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 685 outpatients, the seven dimensions, R² = 0.08 for pain, ΔR² values (0.55, 0.41, 0.38), somatization as most robust predictor, and the reversed-order trauma-diagnosis result all match. The Blais royalty conflict is correctly carried into Caveats.

**Issue A. "Essentially none of the variance"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "your diagnosis explained essentially none of the variance in whether you were suicidal, functioning, or satisfied with life"
- **Abstract says:** "diagnostic categories significantly predicted pain (R2 = 0.08) but did not predict the other four outcome measures."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports non-significance, not effect sizes near zero, for those four outcomes. The actual R² values are unverifiable from the abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "your diagnosis did not significantly predict whether you were suicidal, functioning, or satisfied with life"

**Issue B. SPECTRA identified as the source of the dimensions** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "co-author Mark Blais receives royalties on the SPECTRA measure used to derive dimensions"
- **Abstract says:** dimensions were "derived from commonly used clinical assessment measures"; the conflict statement says Blais "is an author of the SPECTRA: Indices of Psychopathology, and he receives royalties on sales of the SPECTRA."
- **Problem:** The abstract never states that SPECTRA was among the measures used. The royalty interest is real and correctly disclosed, but the link to this study's dimensions is unverifiable from the abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "co-author Mark Blais receives royalties on the SPECTRA: Indices of Psychopathology (whether it was among the measures used here is not stated in the abstract)"

**Issue C. Novelty tag** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "research examining the incremental validity of transdiagnostic dimensions over diagnostic categories remains limited."
- **Problem:** The authors position this as filling a gap and supporting dimensional models, not as contradicting an established prior finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "Novelty:** Fills an evidence gap / supports an existing challenge to categorical diagnosis"

---

### Study 5: Depression may come first and drive complex PTSD, not the other way around
**PMID:** 42594693 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 250, four waves over two years, RI-CLPM, stronger association with DSO than PTSD, DSO → depression from T2 to T4 — all accurate, and the population definition matches the abstract closely.

**Issue A. Headline asserts a one-way relationship the study contradicts** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Depression may come first and drive complex PTSD, not the other way around"
- **Abstract says:** "Depressive symptoms were significantly longitudinally associated with both PTSD and DSO symptoms... Additionally, DSO symptoms were also significantly longitudinally associated with depressive symptoms from T2 to T4."
- **Problem:** The study found associations in both directions, which the digest's own body text correctly calls "a self-sustaining loop rather than a one-way street." The headline's "not the other way around" contradicts both the abstract and the digest body, and "drive" imports causal language into a within-person observational model.
- **Suggested fix:** "Depression may help set off complex PTSD — and then be fed by it"

---

### Study 6: Veterans who broke their own moral code report more feelings of unreality
**PMID:** 41347711 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 189 Israeli male combat veterans, cross-sectional, self-report, PTSD symptoms mediating PMIE exposure → dissociation, and the commission-of-transgressions facet association all match.

**Issue A. The "asymmetry" hook is not in the abstract** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "one specific facet — having committed moral transgressions oneself, as opposed to witnessing or being betrayed — was independently associated with depersonalization and derealization" / "The surprise is the asymmetry: what a soldier did, not what was done to them, tracked with feeling unreal."
- **Abstract says:** "one of the facets of exposure to PMIEs, the commission of moral transgressions, was significantly associated with depersonalization/derealization symptoms."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports one facet as significantly associated; it does not report that the betrayal or witnessing facets were non-significant. The contrast that carries the whole pitch is unverifiable from the abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "one facet — having committed moral transgressions oneself — was significantly associated with depersonalization and derealization (whether the betrayal and witnessing facets were non-significant is not reported in the abstract; confirm from the full text before pitching the contrast)"

**Issue B. "Independently"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "was independently associated with depersonalization and derealization"
- **Abstract says:** "was significantly associated with depersonalization/derealization symptoms"
- **Problem:** "Independently" implies adjustment for the other PMIE facets, which the abstract does not state.
- **Suggested fix:** "was significantly associated with depersonalization and derealization"

---

### Study 7: Whether you "have PTSD" can depend on which scoring rule your clinician uses
**PMID:** 42635035 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 248, mean age 36.5, 79% female, CAPS-5 plus PCL-5, good internal consistency/test-retest/convergent validity with limited specificity, 18–38% classification range, thresholds 31–33 — all accurate.

**Issue A. Screening classification described as diagnosis** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "a diagnosis rate that swings from 18% to 38% based on the scoring model" and headline "Whether you 'have PTSD' can depend on which scoring rule your clinician uses"
- **Abstract says:** "Model-derived probable PTSD classification rates varied substantially (18-38%) across symptom-cluster algorithms," and concludes the PCL-5 "should not be used as a stand-alone diagnostic tool."
- **Problem:** The swinging figure is a self-report screening classification rate, not a diagnosis rate, and no clinician assigns a PTSD diagnosis by choosing a PCL-5 cluster algorithm. As written, a reader could conclude their diagnosis is an artefact of a scoring choice.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Whether a questionnaire flags you as probably having PTSD depends on how the symptoms are grouped." Body: "a probable-PTSD screening rate that swings from 18% to 38% based on the scoring model — the authors stress the PCL-5 should not be used as a stand-alone diagnostic tool."

---

### Study 8: Avoidance may be the weakest sign of PTSD in refugees
**PMID:** 42635367 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 267, 61% male, mean age 25.2, CFA/SEM, the three clusters as stronger indicators than avoidance, and the non-significant resilience–avoidance association all match.

**Issue A. Hyperarousal singled out as the dominant cluster** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "while hyperarousal — plausibly a rational response to continuing insecurity about status, housing, and family — dominated"
- **Abstract says:** Results: "Hyperarousal, negative alterations in cognition and mood (NACM), and re-experiencing symptom clusters were stronger indicators of PTSD, compared to avoidance." Plain Language Summary: "Negative alterations in cognition and mood, hyperarousal, and re-experiencing symptoms were respectively stronger indicators of PTSD than avoidance."
- **Problem:** The abstract's two orderings differ, and the plain-language summary places NACM first. The abstract supports "hyperarousal is an important cluster," not that it dominated the others.
- **Suggested fix:** "while hyperarousal and negative alterations in cognition and mood — plausibly reflecting continuing insecurity about status, housing, and family — carried far more weight"

**Issue B. Headline generalizes to refugees as a group** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Avoidance may be the weakest sign of PTSD in refugees"
- **Abstract says:** "267 (61% male) young adults (Mage = 25.21) with a refugee background who had experienced trauma," in Sweden; "Further research is warranted to replicate and extend these results."
- **Problem:** The finding comes from young adults with a refugee background in one host country; the headline reads as a property of refugees generally.
- **Suggested fix:** "Avoidance may be the weakest sign of PTSD in young refugees resettled in Sweden"

---

### Study 9: Childhood maltreatment predicts depression severity — inflammation does not
**PMID:** 42673683 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 133, first-episode drug-naïve, hs-CRP ≥10 mg/L excluded, β = 0.362 (PHQ-9) and 0.288 (MADRS), eveningness significant for PHQ-9 only, hs-CRP not independently associated, BMI the strongest correlate of CRP — all accurate.

**Issue A. "Predicts" in a cross-sectional study** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Childhood maltreatment predicts depression severity — inflammation does not"
- **Abstract says:** "This cross-sectional study included 133 first episode drug-naïve patients... Childhood maltreatment showed consistent associations across self-reported and clinician-rated severity."
- **Problem:** Nothing was predicted over time; these are cross-sectional associations, and the abstract uses "associated with" throughout.
- **Suggested fix:** "Childhood maltreatment tracks depression severity — inflammation doesn't"

**Issue B. Severity restriction omitted from the null's conditions** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "narrow BMI distribution may have masked a real association"
- **Abstract says:** "In this sample, with moderate-to-severe depression and a relatively narrow BMI distribution, no independent association between hs-CRP and depressive severity was observed."
- **Problem:** The authors condition their null on two sample features; the digest carries only one. A restricted severity range limits the variance available to detect a CRP–severity association.
- **Suggested fix:** "sample restricted to moderate-to-severe depression and a narrow BMI distribution — either may have masked a real association"

---

### Study 10: A history of childhood adversity doesn't stop chronic pain treatment working
**PMID:** 42166956 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 324, 5-week interdisciplinary inpatient program in Germany, three ACE groups, 83.3% ≥1 ACE, 18.5% ≥4, higher baseline distress, emotional abuse as a predictor — all accurate.

**Issue A. Equivalent improvement across ACE groups is not reported** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "all groups improved significantly over the program, with the high-ACE group still ending at higher absolute distress" / "people carrying four or more childhood adversities improved as much as everyone else" / "early adversity set the starting point, not the slope of recovery"
- **Abstract says:** "While patients showed significant improvement in these measures by the end of the rehabilitation program, those with more ACEs continued to report higher levels of distress."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports improvement for the sample and persistently higher distress in the high-ACE group. It does not report a group-by-time interaction test or per-group change scores, so "improved as much as everyone else" and "not the slope of recovery" — the entire hook — are unverifiable from the abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "patients improved significantly over the programme, though those with more ACEs still ended at higher absolute distress; whether the size of improvement was equivalent across ACE groups is not reported in the abstract"

**Issue B. Authors' conclusion points the other way** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "It complicates the fatalistic reading of the ACE literature"
- **Abstract says:** "Patients with a history of multiple ACEs experience greater initial distress and require more comprehensive, trauma-informed and psychosomatically oriented care approaches to achieve optimal rehabilitation outcomes."
- **Problem:** The authors' takeaway is that high-ACE patients need more intensive care, not that adversity is unproblematic for treatment response. The digest's optimistic frame should acknowledge this.
- **Suggested fix:** Add: "The authors' own conclusion is that multiple-ACE patients need more comprehensive, trauma-informed care to reach good outcomes."

---

### Study 11: A 17-minute video handed out during a forensic exam may help after sexual assault
**PMID:** 42635087 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 50 (25/25), SAMFE within seven days, SMART design, n = 36 re-randomized (18/18), 80% rating STAR extremely acceptable, 94%/90% retention — all accurate, and the pitch correctly warns that efficacy was not tested.

**Issue A. Headline implies benefit that was not measured** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "A 17-minute video handed out during a forensic exam may help after sexual assault"
- **Abstract says:** "This study examined the acceptability and feasibility of a 17-minute video... STAR and TextSTAR are acceptable and feasible brief interventions for recent sexual assault survivors."
- **Problem:** No symptom outcomes were tested against the control arms; "may help" is exactly the inference a feasibility trial cannot support, and the headline is what an editor reads first even though the body and Caveats are careful.
- **Suggested fix:** "A 17-minute video handed out during a forensic exam proves deliverable — and welcome — after sexual assault"

---

### Study 12: A new screening tool aims to catch PTSD that starts in pregnancy, not just at birth
**PMID:** 41936021 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

25 candidate items, EFA n = 114, 17-item two-factor solution, 68.36% of variance, α = .954 and .897, ROC n = 52, cutoff ≥11, 90.9% sensitivity, 61% specificity, validation pending — all accurate.

**Issue A. Novelty tag** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Novelty:** First-in-class"
- **Abstract says:** "While existing perinatal PTSD tools show validity, they vary in diagnostic agreement, and most are focused on PTSD following childbirth."
- **Problem:** Perinatal PTSD screening tools already exist; this one extends the window across conception and pregnancy. "First-in-class" overstates it.
- **Suggested fix:** "Novelty:** Extends an existing tool class (first to span conception, pregnancy and postpartum)"

**Issue B. Specific missed presentations not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "so PTSD following miscarriage, fertility treatment, or a frightening pregnancy is routinely missed"
- **Abstract says:** "Unfortunately, gaps remain in practice for identifying perinatal PTSD," with the tool aimed at events "during conception, pregnancy and the postpartum."
- **Problem:** The named examples and the claim that they are "routinely missed" are unverifiable from the abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "so trauma arising at conception or during pregnancy — not just at birth — falls outside what current screening asks about"

---

### Study 13: Neglect, not the drinking itself, links parental substance abuse to child exploitation
**PMID:** 41974448 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 738 children aged 10–18 in Lahore urban slums, directly exposed to paternal substance abuse, SEM, neglect as mediator, gender control barely changing the model — all accurate.

**Issue A. Headline and pitch imply full mediation** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Neglect, not the drinking itself, links parental substance abuse to child exploitation" / "it wasn't the father's substance use that tracked with exploitation so much as the collapse of supervision that followed it"
- **Abstract says:** "PSA was significantly associated with both CSE and CED and was strongly linked to CN. CN significantly predicted both forms of child vulnerability and mediated the relationships between PSA and these outcomes... all paths remained significant and consistent in direction."
- **Problem:** Paternal substance abuse retained significant direct associations with both outcomes; the abstract describes mediation, not that the direct link disappeared. "Not the drinking itself" reverses the emphasis.
- **Suggested fix:** "Caregiver neglect is the link between paternal substance abuse and child exploitation" / "the father's substance use was still directly associated with exploitation, but much of the relationship ran through the collapse of supervision"

**Issue B. "Parental" and "drinking"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Neglect, not the drinking itself, links parental substance abuse to child exploitation"
- **Abstract says:** "paternal substance abuse (PSA)"; children "directly exposed to paternal substance abuse."
- **Problem:** The exposure measured was paternal, not parental (the digest body gets this right), and "substance abuse" is not specifically alcohol.
- **Suggested fix:** "Neglect, not the substance use itself, links paternal addiction to child exploitation"

---

### Study 14: Rejection and violence, not everyday discrimination, drive trauma symptoms in trans people
**PMID:** 42658623 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

PRISMA-guided meta-analysis, 13 sources / 10 unique samples, GMSR measure, r = .39 rejection, .36 violence, .25 discrimination — all accurate.

**Issue A. Causal verb and a false negative in the headline** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Rejection and violence, not everyday discrimination, drive trauma symptoms in trans people"
- **Abstract says:** "a small mean effect size was found for the association between PTSS and discrimination (r = .25)... These results highlight the magnitude of the association between distal gender minority stressors and PTSS, particularly for experiences of rejection and violence."
- **Problem:** Two errors in one line: "drive" is causal language for a meta-analysis of cross-sectional associations (the digest's own pitch says "Stick to association; none of these are longitudinal"), and discrimination did show a small but real association, so "not everyday discrimination" misstates the result as a null.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rejection and violence track trauma symptoms in trans people more strongly than everyday discrimination"

**Issue B. Criterion A claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The authors argue these stressors sit outside the conventional Criterion A definition of a traumatic event"
- **Abstract says:** "The findings have implications for improving diagnostic procedures and treatment planning for the TGD population"; the title refers to "Broadening conceptualizations of trauma."
- **Problem:** Criterion A is never mentioned in the abstract. The direction of the authors' argument is consistent with the digest, but the specific claim is unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "The authors argue for broadening how trauma is conceptualized for this population" — and confirm the Criterion A framing from the full text.

**Issue C. Size comparison to "recognized stressors"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "show associations with post-traumatic stress symptoms comparable in size to many recognized stressors"
- **Abstract says:** reports only the three effect sizes; no benchmarking against other stressors.
- **Problem:** No comparison to Criterion A events or other stressors appears in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "show moderate associations with post-traumatic stress symptoms despite not meeting the diagnostic threshold for a traumatic event"

---

### Study 15: Earthquake survivors who build a "trauma identity" fare worse
**PMID:** 42036873 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 285 (65.3% female), 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes, cross-sectional SEM, the memory → cognitions → identity/safety-seeking → symptoms → mental health pathway, and the identity/PTSD versus safety-seeking/CPTSD split all match.

**Issue A. Headline asserts an outcome the design can't order in time** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Earthquake survivors who build a 'trauma identity' fare worse"
- **Abstract says:** "A cross-sectional design was employed... These mediators were positively associated with PTSD and CPTSD symptoms, which negatively predicted mental health."
- **Problem:** "Build" and "fare worse" imply a process unfolding over time toward a later outcome. Everything was measured at one time point, which the digest's own Caveats note ("SEM path direction assumed rather than tested"), so the headline sits at odds with the caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "Earthquake survivors with a stronger 'trauma identity' report worse mental health"

---

### Study 16: Trouble naming your feelings may link childhood trauma to a stiffer heartbeat
**PMID:** 42579979 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 152 university students, mean age 22.19, ECG-derived HRV (RMSSD), childhood trauma negatively associated with HRV, serial mediation via alexithymia and anxiety — all accurate, and the pitch's warning against "childhood trauma damages your heart" is appropriate.

**Issue A. "Accounted for" is stronger than the abstract's wording** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Serial mediation analysis indicated that alexithymia and anxiety accounted for the association both independently and in sequence."
- **Abstract says:** "Serial mediation analysis indicated that alexithymia and anxiety symptoms were statistically associated with the relationship between childhood trauma and HRV through both independent and sequential indirect pathways."
- **Problem:** The authors deliberately use hedged, association-only phrasing ("Within a cross-sectional associational framework"). "Accounted for" implies the pathways explain the association.
- **Suggested fix:** "Serial mediation analysis found alexithymia and anxiety statistically associated with the trauma–HRV relationship through both independent and sequential indirect pathways."

---

### Study 17: How a therapist asks questions changes the trauma story a client tells
**PMID:** 42684797 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

62 sessions, 24 client interviews, participants from Iraq/Afghanistan/Syria/Lebanon in Isfahan, micro- plus macro-level analysis, the interpretive-question and open-ended-prompt findings, and the multilingual/cultural modulation all match. The digest correctly notes the study measured coherence, not accuracy.

**Issue A. "Reliably reshapes"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "while this work suggests retelling in supportive settings reliably reshapes narratives"
- **Abstract says:** "interpretive questions and reformulative practices appeared associated with changes in temporal sequencing, evaluative framing and narrative coherence"
- **Problem:** "Reliably" claims consistency and predictability that a qualitative, single-site study with no control condition cannot establish — and it undercuts the digest's own careful framing elsewhere in the entry.
- **Suggested fix:** "while this work suggests retelling in supportive settings can reshape how a narrative is sequenced and framed"

**Issue B. "Refugees and immigrants"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "62 therapy sessions and 24 client interviews with refugees and immigrants from Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, and Lebanon"
- **Abstract says:** "How therapist discourse shapes trauma narratives in immigrant clients... 24 client interviews with participants from Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria and Lebanon"
- **Problem:** The abstract describes immigrant clients; refugee status is not stated and matters because the wider angle turns on asylum procedure.
- **Suggested fix:** "62 therapy sessions and 24 client interviews with immigrant clients from Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, and Lebanon"

### Study 18: Who drops out of trauma treatment isn't predicted by how ill they are
**PMID:** 42222912 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract: N = 76 women hospitalized 2019–2023, 96% with PTSD / 74% ED / 70% both, 43.4% premature termination, associations with sexual risk-taking, impulsive departures and fewer prior hospitalizations, no sociodemographic or symptom-severity differences, and comparable outcomes for those who left and returned. The plain-language summary supports both the "behavioural indicators, not initial symptom severity" framing and the re-engagement angle, and the 4/10 fit score is well calibrated to a small single-center sample. One note: the "retrospective chart-based design" characterization in Caveats is unverifiable from abstract only, but it errs on the conservative side.
